title: Bug Triage — Payments Incident
description: Duplicate charges on renewal. Immediate mitigation and follow-up.
transcript: Right, everyone's here. Yuki, you raised it — go.
We've got customers being charged twice on renewal. Four confirmed so far this morning.
First ticket came in at seven forty. But the charges are dated yesterday evening, so it's been happening for at least twelve hours.
Two mid-market, two small. No enterprise yet, but that might just be timing — enterprise renewals cluster at month end.
So this could get much worse in about a week.
James, do we know what's happening?
I've got a theory but I want to be careful because I've only had it for ten minutes.
Theories are fine as long as we label them.
The renewal job retries on failure. If the payment provider times out, we retry.
The problem is that a timeout doesn't mean the charge failed. It means we didn't hear back.
So we charge, don't hear, and charge again.
Is there an idempotency key on the request?
There is, but I think it's being regenerated on retry. Which makes it useless.
I want to confirm before we act on it. Give me fifteen minutes with the logs.
Take it. Meanwhile — Yuki, how are we handling the affected customers?
I've refunded the duplicates manually. It's four accounts, it's manageable.
Have you told them, or are you waiting?
I've replied to the ones who wrote in. I haven't proactively contacted anyone who hasn't noticed.
I'd contact them. Finding a duplicate charge yourself after we knew is much worse than hearing from us first.
Agreed, I just wanted the call.
You've got it. I'll draft the message so it's consistent.
Good. While James is digging — do we stop the renewal job?
What's the cost of stopping it?
Renewals don't process. Nobody loses access immediately, there's a grace period, so the blast radius of stopping is small.
Then stop it. A delayed renewal is an email; a double charge is a chargeback.
That's a good way to frame it. I'll stop it now.
How long can it stay stopped?
A few days without anyone noticing. A week and we'd have a revenue recognition problem.
Back. It's confirmed, and it's slightly worse than I said.
The idempotency key is generated inside the retry loop, so every attempt gets a fresh one. That part I had right.
What I missed is that the retry is also triggered by a 5xx from our own queue, not just from the provider.
So we can retry a charge that definitely succeeded, because our own infrastructure hiccupped after the fact.
So a customer could in principle be charged four times.
In principle, yes. In practice I've only seen doubles.
I'd like to check that rather than assume it.
That's fair. I can query for any account with more than two charges in a twenty-four hour window.
Do that first, actually. Before the fix. If there's a triple out there I want to know now.
Move the key generation outside the loop, so all attempts share one key. That's a two-line change.
They do. Same key within twenty-four hours returns the original charge rather than making a new one.
Then that's the fix. Two lines, but I want it reviewed properly given where we are.
Is there a wider version of this problem? Other jobs that retry against external services?
Almost certainly. The renewal job is the one with money attached, which is why we noticed.
That's an audit, not a fix. Let's do the fix today and the audit properly afterwards.
As long as the audit actually happens.
I'll raise the ticket now so it exists.
What do I tell customers about why it happened?
Keep it short and true. A retry in our billing system charged some customers twice, we've refunded it, we've stopped it recurring.
Not unless they ask. If they ask, tell them exactly what James just told us.
Right. Ordering — James checks for triples, then ships the two-line fix with review. Yuki and Elena handle communications. I'll restart the job once the fix is deployed.
How long until we know about triples?
Then let's reconvene at half nine. Thanks everyone, this was quick and useful.

summary.overview: Four customers were charged twice on renewal, with charges dating back at least twelve hours before the first ticket. James traced it to an idempotency key regenerated inside the retry loop, made worse by retries also firing on 5xx responses from our own queue — meaning a charge that definitely succeeded could be repeated up to three times. The renewal job was stopped immediately on the reasoning that a delayed renewal is an email while a double charge is a chargeback. The fix is a two-line change moving key generation outside the loop, gated on first confirming no account was charged more than twice.
summary.gist: Duplicate renewal charges from a regenerated idempotency key; job stopped, two-line fix pending a triple-charge check.

outline.title: The fix and the wider audit

bullets: Four confirmed duplicate charges; two mid-market, two small.
Charges predate the first ticket by at least twelve hours.
No enterprise accounts yet — but enterprise renewals cluster at month end, roughly a week away.
The idempotency key is generated inside the retry loop, so every attempt gets a fresh key.
Retries also fire on 5xx from our own queue, so a charge that succeeded can still be repeated.
Three retries means a customer could in principle be charged four times.
Stopped immediately — a grace period means nobody loses access.
Framing that decided it: a delayed renewal is an email, a double charge is a chargeback.
Safe for a few days; a week creates a revenue recognition problem.

notes.chapter: The fix and the wider audit
bullets: Two-line change moving key generation outside the retry loop; the provider honours a repeated key for 24 hours.
Reviewed rather than hot-fixed, given the context.
Other jobs retrying against external services likely share the flaw — raised as a separate audit so it is not lost.

action_items.text: Query for any account charged more than twice in a 24-hour window
Move idempotency key generation outside the retry loop
Proactively contact affected customers who have not written in
Audit every job that retries against an external service for the same flaw
Restart the renewal job once the fix is deployed and verified
Write a template for billing incident customer communications
